original.title: CDP request futures retained after timeout
original.evidence: Pending map insertion precedes send and wait_for; only receiving matching reply pops it. No finally cleanup.
original.trigger: Repeated requests time out or ws.send raises without replies.
original.impact: Pending map grows without bound for lifetime of page.

close cancels receive task and closes WebSocket without clearing the map.

A late matching response does remove its entry; the failure case requires absent responses.

original.title: Browser launch timeout leaves browser process alive
original.evidence: launch returns False on endpoint timeout; __aenter__ raises and __aexit__ is never entered.
original.trigger: Browser process starts but DevTools readiness fails.
original.impact: Browser child and profile remain until explicit close or process teardown.

history.rationale: After Popen succeeds, endpoint timeout or a later exception returns False without terminating the process. __aenter__ then raises; its __aexit__ cleanup is not entered. A failed context-manager launch can therefore retain its browser child until separate close or process termination. TemporaryDirectory finalization may eventually clean the profile; indefinite profile retention is not asserted.

original.title: Non-persist witness digest silently replaces SHA256 with XOR
original.evidence: cfg(not(cortex-persist)) ignores domain and XOR-folds payload into32bytes; PhysicalResourceWitness uses it at1689.
original.trigger: Library built without cortex-persist; same-inode64byte content mutated at positions0 and32 by toggling low bit from zero to one.
original.impact: Both paired contributions change identically so digest remains unchanged; physical witness can miss content mutation. This is an API configuration issue, not proof of a deployed bypass.

history.rationale: The non-cortex-persist branch returns an XOR fold and explicitly discards the domain, despite the SHA-256 API/name. For a 64-byte zero payload, setting bytes 0 and 32 to 1 changes contributions from 0 XOR 32 to 1 XOR 33, leaving the digest identical. The witness detects mutation only by digest or inode inequality, so same-inode paired edits are invisible in that configuration. Static reasoning only; no Rust binary or protected file was executed.

source_checks.observation: Feature-disabled branch ignores domain and returns a weak XOR fold.
Mutation predicate compares digest/inode; file reader invokes the helper.
Default and microkernel enable cortex-persist; it gates sha2 dependency.

guards: Default and microkernel Cargo features include cortex-persist, whose branch uses SHA-256 with domain and length.
O_NOFOLLOW and inode comparison protect other failure modes but not equal-inode XOR collisions.
Finding applies to builds explicitly omitting cortex-persist; no default-build bypass is claimed.

original.title: Auto purge unlinks SQLite WAL files without checkpoint or connection coordination
original.evidence: Lines 23-24 delete all *.db-shm and *.db-wal recursively from cwd. strict_reviewer.py:155 calls run_auto_purge before git add/commit; no SQLite checkpoint or exclusive ownership is checked.
original.trigger: Strict reviewer or another caller runs purge while a database has committed WAL content not checkpointed into its main database.
original.impact: Committed database contents can be lost or concurrent clients disrupted; WAL files are persistent transaction state rather than disposable caches.

history.rationale: run_auto_purge recursively unlinks every *.db-shm and *.db-wal beneath the working directory with no database ownership, checkpoint or connection coordination. A live WAL can contain committed pages not yet in the main database, so this deletion can lose committed state or disrupt other clients. strict_reviewer invokes the helper before committing, although earlier reviewer work can itself fail; public helper reachability alone is sufficient for the hazard. No purge or database deletion was executed.

Reviewer stops its own actor and later invokes the global purge before Git add/commit.

guards: OS permissions limit which files find can delete.
The helper uses check=False, with no liveness or checkpoint guard.
The caller stopping its own ledger does not establish exclusive ownership of every database under cwd.

original.title: Backward conditioning uses the initial prior at the wrong timestep

history.rationale: For time-zero prior [1,0], target 1 and observed B at time 2, the exact function returns [1,0], while independent path enumeration gives approximately [0.470588,0.529412]. This reproduces the mathematical mismatch under the candidate interpretation. However, the function documents pi0 only as a prior distribution, with no explicit time origin; confirm that contract before treating initial-prior propagation as an unconditional API defect. audit_system reuses one pi0 across targets, supporting but not conclusively defining the time-zero interpretation.

history.rationale: The primitive docstring still does not explicitly define whether pi0 is at time zero or at target_t, so the stronger statement that every positive-target single call is wrong is not established. However, the canonical local MODULE.md:42-45 defines all retrodictions as conditionals of one joint process rho on the shared history, and audit_system/CLI accept multiple targets while passing the same unrestricted prior vector to every target. An independent exact-source fixture with T=[[0.8,0.2],[0.1,0.9]], pi0=[1,0], observation S2=B and targets [0,1] returns q0=q1=[1,0]. For any one Markov joint process with this T and observation, the function's own q0 fixes q1 through the Bayesian bridge identity: q1(j)=sum_i q0(i)*T(i,j)*T(j,B)/(T^2)(i,B). Exact rational evaluation requires q1=[8/17,9/17], contradicting the returned [1,0]. This confirms a multi-target temporal-prior coherence defect without assuming pi0's time origin. A stationary-prior control [1/3,2/3] satisfies the identity, showing the scope rather than claiming universal failure. Single-target callers supplying the target marginal can be correct; the public batch must either define a common initial time and propagate its prior, accept target-indexed marginals, or explicitly restrict/check stationary priors. No product or protected runtime was executed, and no remediation was performed.

Single-writer processing does not repair predecessors captured during ingestion.

original.title: Stale lock eviction can delete a live replacement lock
original.evidence: exists/getmtime/unlink occur separately; eviction uses age alone, with no owner or inode validation; release_lock unlinks any existing lock.
original.trigger: Two contenders observe an old lock; one removes it and acquires a new lock before the other performs its already-planned unlink. A live operation longer than 300 seconds is another eviction trigger.
original.impact: Both processes may believe they own the workspace mutation lock. No mutation consumer was found in targeted scripts/tests search; scope is correctness of the helper itself.

history.rationale: Stale detection reads existence and mtime separately from unlink. One contender may replace a stale lock before another unlinks based on the old observation; release similarly removes whichever lock occupies the path. Age alone also evicts a still-running operation after 300 seconds. Targeted search found no external mutation consumer, so impact is established for the helper contract, not a proven deployed race.

source_checks.observation: Age-based eviction precedes O_EXCL acquisition; no owner or inode is checked.
Release unlinks any existing lock, and the CLI immediately releases after acquisition.

guards: O_EXCL makes initial creation atomic.
Written PID/EPOCH are not read to validate liveness or ownership, and no heartbeat exists.

original.title: Stack slots grow beyond the reserved 256-byte frame
original.evidence: The prologue reserves 256 bytes. get_offset starts at 16 and increments by 8 without a bound or frame sizing pass; Alloc and Free emit calls.
original.trigger: Compile a block containing at least 32 distinct registers followed by Alloc or Free.
original.impact: The 32nd slot is rbp-264, exactly where call pushes its return address when rsp=rbp-256; slots collide with call data and program values are corrupted. More registers write below the frame.

history.rationale: Stack slots begin at 16 and grow by 8 without a frame-sizing pass or bound, while the prologue reserves a fixed 256 bytes then aligns rsp. The original exact 32nd-slot return-address claim is inaccurate: with the emitted aligned stack_top, push rbp and and rsp,-16, rsp is rbp-264 and a call writes rbp-272, the 33rd slot. At least 33 live slots followed by Alloc/Free can overwrite a stored value. No native assembly was compiled or run; this is a public backend emission defect.

source_checks.observation: Monotonic slot allocation is unbounded.
Aligned stack_top plus push/sub/and yields effective 264-byte frame.
ConstInt creates a slot; Alloc emits a call.
Free also emits a call.
Backend is publicly exported; no caller-side slot restriction here.

guards: The 16-byte alignment buys one additional slot, not an unbounded frame.
Targeted backend caller search found its definition/export, not a demonstrated deployed native path.

original.title: Arithmetic overflow escapes VM fail-closed handling
original.evidence: mul_scalar multiplies accumulated u128 units without checked_mul and casts seconds to u64; add at line 35 also uses unchecked u64 addition. execute directly calls both. ffi.rs:143-163 exposes execution through extern C without panic handling.
original.trigger: Repeated SexaMulRational or SexaAdd instructions exceed the seconds range; registers are also public to Rust callers.
original.impact: Release arithmetic can wrap or truncate and return success with an incorrect result; checked builds panic rather than poisoning the manifest, and panic crossing the C ABI can abort the host process.

history.rationale: SexaRegister.add uses unchecked u64 addition, while mul_scalar uses unchecked u128 multiplication then truncates the quotient with as u64. For example seconds=2^63 and factor=2 already produce a quotient of 2^64 that truncates to zero without needing u128 overflow. execute calls these helpers directly rather than returning an arithmetic error through poison_and_abort. Larger unchecked additions/products can wrap with overflow checks disabled or panic with them enabled; b60_run_bytecode has an extern C boundary and no panic catcher. Native panic/abort behavior was not executed, and no deployment build profile was assumed.

Normal fail-closed handling requires returning through poison_and_abort.

C ABI directly calls execute and handles Result only.

original.title: Out-of-range jumps return successful execution
original.evidence: Jump assigns the decoded u16 directly to pc; the execute loop only checks pc < bytecode.len() and returns Ok after it ends. Conditional jump branches do the same. ffi.rs:154-160 converts Ok to return code 0.
original.trigger: Bytecode containing a jump target beyond the supplied buffer.
original.impact: Malformed control flow is accepted as successful completion with a running manifest, rather than rejected.

history.rationale: Jump, JumpIfZero and JumpIfNotZero validate availability of encoded operands but never validate the decoded target. A taken jump beyond bytecode.len() sets pc beyond the loop boundary; the next loop check ends execution and returns Ok while manifest remains RUNNING and is_halted remains false. b60_run_bytecode converts that Ok to 0. This statically establishes acceptance of out-of-buffer control flow; no native VM run was performed.

original.title: KL computation compares histograms with incompatible bin edges
original.evidence: np.histogram(point_cloud,bins=50,density=True) and np.histogram(reconstructed_cloud,bins=50,density=True) independently choose edges, then their array indices are compared as the same events.
original.trigger: Input and reconstructed clouds have different ranges, including translated distributions of the same shape.
original.impact: Reported KL can hide displaced probability mass or compare unrelated intervals; returned calibration metrics are incorrect.

history.rationale: calibrate_sheaf_operator independently bins both arrays with bins=50 and no common range or edges, then compares those histograms indexwise as P and Q. Translated equal-shape samples can have identical per-array counts despite occupying disjoint intervals, yielding a near-zero KL for different events. Clipping and normalization do not repair incompatible bin supports. Confirmed in the demonstration/calibration function, without claiming measured physical energy.

Two independently derived histogram grids feed reported KL and energy-bound values.

original.title: Shutdown stops consumer before draining its queue
original.evidence: stop() sets _stop_event before awaiting queue.join(); _worker loops only while that event is unset (line 366).
original.trigger: Call stop() with at least one queued event before the worker consumes it.

original.title: Persistent retry deadlines use a clock that resets at reboot
original.evidence: Worker compares next_retry_at to time.monotonic at 43-54 and stores it at 77; producer pulmones.py:87 stores time.monotonic()+delay in SQLite.
original.trigger: Reboot after queueing a task when the previous uptime was long.
original.impact: Persisted deadlines remain in the previous boot clock domain and can postpone retries for the old uptime duration.

history.rationale: The persistent SQLite deadline stores time.monotonic()+delay and is compared against a later boot/process clock with no boot identity or rebasing. A reboot that restarts the monotonic epoch can defer old retries by the previous uptime, or otherwise alter the intended delay. Persistence of the raw monotonic reading does not create a durable clock.

The producer persists REAL next_retry_at and computes it from time.monotonic().

guards: Both producer and consumer use the same clock within a boot.
No boot marker, recovery rebasing or durable wall-clock conversion is present.

original.title: Worker suppresses encoder failure and can deliver truncated video
original.evidence: The frame write catches BrokenPipeError/IOError and breaks at 428-432; ffmpeg_proc.wait() at 442 has its return code discarded. The worker returns normally; parent only checks Python child return codes at 700-704 before concatenation.
